Samir / Elena — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap + proposed next steps from our side so we can align on SLOs and the technical deep-dive: 

Demo highlights (short):
- Your core use case: interactive search + real-time assistant embedded in product UI (mixed text + short code snippets).
- Expected peak traffic in pilot: ~250 concurrent users, average session generates ~3 streaming responses (~60 tokens initial chunk + incremental chunks).

Performance asks you called out:
- Target perceived latency (time-to-first-chunk): <= 150 ms for 95th pct under pilot load (US region).
- Sustained throughput target: 50 streaming responses/sec with bursts to 120 rps during spikes.
- Concurrency: up to 300 concurrent connections during marketing events.
- Chunking behavior: client prefers small first chunk (~40–80 tokens), then 20–40 token incremental chunks every 80–120 ms.

Our initial qualification notes / constraints:
- We can hit ~100–120 ms TTFT for a small model variant on our hosted fleet under controlled prefix caching and warm KV cache (needs validation with your payload).
- Sustaining 50 rps streaming with <150 ms 95p TTFT will require either dedicated capacity or reserved burst capacity on our shared pool; we estimate a Dedicated slot (x1) for safety during pilot.
- WebSocket vs SSE: WS preferred if you need two-way control messages (client ack, chunk-level resend). SSE is simpler and works well for one-way streaming; cadence control is server-driven.

Immediate asks / next steps:
1) Can you share a tiny representative sample payload set (5–10 typical prompts + average token counts) and one worst-case prompt? Attach to HubSpot or email — I attached a requirements matrix template to this thread.
2) Confirm whether you need client-initiated chunk ACKs or just ordered SSE/WebSocket delivery (no ACKs).
3) We'll schedule a 60-min technical deep-dive (SRE + runtime engineer + your engineering lead) to go over perf knobs. Proposed slot: Tue 6 Oct, 10:00–11:00 PT.

Attachments: [attachment: nebula_req_matrix.xlsx (xlsx, 18KB)]
Recording: [attachment: demo-recording.mp4 (mp4, 8MB)]

Thanks — I’ll loop Ben for the runtime/ops details and Neha for pricing/DED sizing.

—Lauren

Thanks Lauren — appreciated the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Payloads: attaching a sanitized set of 6 typical prompts + one large context prompt (worst-case) to this reply. You should see token counts in the spreadsheet.
- ACKs: we don't need explicit chunk ACKs right now; we want ordered delivery and the ability to request a resend if a chunk drops (rare).
- Chunk cadence: ideal is ~100 ms between increments for a smooth typing experience; 80 ms is okay if it doesn't burn rate too fast.
- Regional requirement: must run in us-west-2 for data residency during pilot.

Accept Tue 6 Oct 10:00 PT for the deep-dive. Please include whoever owns KV cache mechanics and the batching strategy.

Quick Q: are there any known issues with small-first-chunk designs and quantized models? We observed earlier that very small initial chunks sometimes increase latency due to repeated scheduling.

—Samir

Lauren / Samir — quick technical note ahead of tomorrow's deep-dive: 

- Small-first-chunk + quantized model behavior: true — scheduling overhead can dominate when the first chunk is below ~40 tokens. We usually recommend first chunk in the 40–80 token range to amortize model invocation and avoid repeated kernel loads.
- Prefix/KV caching: if Nebula can provide representative prefixes (session-level identifiers or repeated system prompts), we can warm KV cache and cut TTFT by ~20–40 ms depending on model size.
- Batching and concurrency: continuous batching helps throughput but adds up to ~30–50 ms jitter on single-request TTFT at low concurrency. Dedicated capacity with tuned batching policies reduces jitter significantly.
- WebSocket control channels: we can support a small control channel over WS for explicit retransmit requests; implementing that will add minimal CPU overhead.

Action items I’ll cover tomorrow: kernel selection matrix for quantized variants, empirical numbers from a 50 rps pilot on Dedicated, and a quick checklist for payload sanitization before we run live tests.

—Ben
